tooltips.constructionYear: Enter the original year of construction of the building. Major renovations can be added later. Older buildings are often less well insulated and consume more heating energy.
tooltips.buildingType: Different assumptions are made for single-family and multi-family houses in the calculation, for example regarding floor usage and energy demand.
tooltips.numberOfFloors: Count only floors excluding the basement and unfinished attic spaces. A house with a ground floor and an upper floor has, for example, 2 floors.
tooltips.livingArea: The living area is the heated floor area of your building.

errors.livingAreaMustBePositive: The living area must be greater than 0.

roof.constructionType: What type of roof does your building have?
roof.hasAttic: Does your building have an attic?
roof.year: When was your roof built or last renovated?

tooltips.year: Enter the year the roof was built or last renovated. Older roofs are often poorly insulated and lose more heat to the outside.
tooltips.area: Enter the total area of your roof, excluding window areas. The larger the area, the more important good insulation is.
tooltips.constructionTypeContent: A flat roof is nearly level or only slightly sloped. A pitched roof has a clearly visible slope, e.g. a gable or hip roof. The roof type affects both the roof area and the heat loss of a building: flat roofs (typically solid construction) have a smaller area than pitched roofs (typically timber construction) for the same floor area, and thus different energy properties.
tooltips.hasAttic: Indicate whether your building has an accessible attic space. An existing attic influences the insulation of the top floor ceiling and thus the heat loss through the top of the building.
tooltips.isAtticHeated: Indicate whether the space directly below the roof (attic) is heated.
tooltips.hasInsulation: Existing insulation significantly reduces heat loss. Without insulation, up to 30% of heating energy is lost through the roof.
tooltips.insulationThickness: A thicker insulation layer increases the building's energy efficiency. Depending on the age of the insulation, between 6 cm and 20 cm is common.
tooltips.insulationTypeContent: With above-rafter insulation, the insulation is fitted above the roof rafters. It provides the best thermal protection as no thermal bridges are created by the rafters. With between-rafter insulation, the insulation material is placed between the rafters. This option is more cost-effective but provides slightly less protection due to the rafters acting as thermal bridges.

info.title: Roof
info.description: The roof closes off the building at the top and borders the outside air. The component is highlighted in red in the graphic.
info.imageAlt: Schematic building with the roof highlighted in red

roofWindows.area: What is the total area of your roof windows?
roofWindows.windowType: What type of roof windows are installed?
roofWindows.uValue: Do you know the U-value of your roof windows?
roofWindows.year: When were your roof windows installed or last replaced?

tooltips.year: Older roof windows lose more heat than newer ones.
tooltips.area: Enter the total area of all roof windows. The total area of all roof windows affects heat loss.
tooltips.windowType: Wood and plastic frames provide good insulation. Aluminium and steel frames conduct cold more strongly and are less energy-efficient.
tooltips.uValue: The U-value indicates how much heat can be lost through a component to the surroundings. Lower values mean better insulation. Old single-pane windows have approximately 5.0 W/m²K. Modern triple-glazed windows are around 0.7 W/m²K. You can find the U-value in your window documentation or on the type plate.

errors.areaExceedsRoofArea: The roof-window area must not be greater than the roof area.

info.title: Roof windows
info.description: Roof windows are windows installed in the roof surface. This does not include windows in exterior walls, e.g. in a gable. The components are highlighted in red in the graphic.

topFloor.year: When was your top floor ceiling built or last renovated?
topFloor.area: What is the area of your top floor ceiling?
topFloor.type: What is the construction type of your top floor ceiling?
topFloor.hasInsulation: Is your top floor ceiling insulated?

tooltips.year: Enter the year the ceiling was built or last renovated. The construction year of the ceiling between the living area and the attic helps assess insulation quality. Older ceilings are often uninsulated.
tooltips.area: Enter the area of the ceiling between the living area and the attic in m². The area of the ceiling to the attic determines how much heat can escape from your home into the (usually unheated) attic.
tooltips.type: The construction type of the ceiling affects the thermal insulation and heat storage capacity of the building. Solid ceiling: e.g. concrete or brick. Timber beam ceiling: construction of wooden beams, common in older buildings.
tooltips.hasInsulation: Insulating the ceiling below the attic prevents heat from escaping upwards from your home. This can save up to 15% in heating costs.
tooltips.insulationThickness: A thicker insulation layer increases the building's energy efficiency. Depending on the age of the insulation, between 10 cm and 24 cm is common.

errors.areaExceedsRoofArea: The top-floor ceiling area must not be greater than the roof area.

info.title: Top floor ceiling
info.description: The top floor ceiling separates the heated living space from the unheated attic. The component is highlighted in red in the graphic.
info.imageAlt: Schematic building with the top floor ceiling highlighted in red

outerWall.year: When was your outer wall built or last renovated?
outerWall.area: What is the total area of your heated, free-standing exterior walls?
outerWall.constructionType: What is the construction type of your outer wall?
outerWall.adjacentWallArea: What is the wall area adjacent to neighbouring buildings?

tooltips.year: Enter the year the wall was built or last major facade renovation. Older walls without insulation lose a lot of heat to the outside.
tooltips.area: Enter the free-standing wall area of all heated above-ground floors, including window areas. Walls shared with neighbouring buildings are not included. Include attic walls only if the attic is heated. A manual entry replaces the estimated area.
tooltips.constructionType: Solid walls (e.g. brick or concrete) store heat well.
tooltips.hasInsulation: Up to 40% of heating energy is lost through uninsulated outer walls. Insulation significantly reduces heating costs.
tooltips.adjacentWallArea: This is the wall area directly adjoining neighbouring buildings, including the walls of an unheated attic. These areas have already been deducted from the automatically estimated exterior wall area. Manually changing this value currently does not affect the calculation.
tooltips.insulationThickness: A thicker insulation layer increases the building's energy efficiency. Depending on the age of the insulation, between 4 cm and 14 cm is common.

errors.adjacentAreaExceedsWallArea: The adjacent wall area must not be greater than the building's total wall area, including attic walls.

tooltips.year: This refers to whether the windows were replaced with better-insulated ones or improved in terms of glazing, frame or connection. Pure repairs, new paint or replacing individual fittings do not count.
tooltips.area: Enter the total area of all windows. The total area of all windows affects heat loss through the building envelope.
tooltips.windowType: Wood and plastic frames provide good insulation. Aluminium and steel frames conduct cold more strongly and are less energy-efficient.
tooltips.uValue: The U-value indicates how much heat can be lost through a component to the surroundings. Lower values mean better insulation. Old single-pane windows have approximately 5.0 W/m²K. Modern triple-glazed windows are around 0.7 W/m²K. You can find the U-value in your window documentation or on the type plate.

errors.areaExceedsAvailableWallArea: The window area must not be greater than the wall area enclosing the heated floors.

info.title: Windows
info.description: Windows include all glazed surfaces as well as exterior doors in the exterior walls. This does not include windows in the roof surface. The components are highlighted in red in the graphic.
info.imageAlt: Schematic building with the windows and exterior door highlighted in red

tooltips.hasBasement: Indicate whether your building has a basement. A basement below the living areas affects thermal insulation and thus your energy demand, especially if it is unheated.
tooltips.isBasementHeated: With an unheated basement, insulating the basement ceiling is particularly worthwhile to prevent cold from rising into the living areas.

area.default: Enter the area of the basement ceiling. The area affects how much heat can be lost through the lower building boundary.
area.heated: Enter the area of the basement floor. The area affects how much heat can be lost through the lower building boundary.
area.noBasement: Enter the area of the ground floor. The area affects how much heat can be lost through the lower building boundary.

year.default: Enter the year the basement ceiling was built or last renovated. Older, uninsulated basement ceilings allow cold to rise into the living areas.
year.heated: Enter the year the basement floor was built or last renovated. Older, uninsulated basement floors allow cold to rise into the living areas.
year.noBasement: Enter the year the floor was built or last renovated. Older, uninsulated floors allow cold to rise into the living areas.

constructionType.default: Solid concrete ceilings can be well insulated and store heat better. Timber beam ceilings have poorer insulation properties.
constructionType.heated: Solid concrete floors can be well insulated and store heat better. Timber beam floors have poorer insulation properties.
constructionType.noBasement: Solid concrete floors can be well insulated and store heat better. Timber beam floors have poorer insulation properties.

hasInsulation.default: Insulating the basement ceiling helps retain heat in the building. This keeps floors warmer and can reduce heating costs.
hasInsulation.heated: Insulating the basement floor helps retain heat in the building. This keeps floors warmer and can reduce heating costs.
hasInsulation.noBasement: Insulating the floor helps retain heat in the building. This keeps floors warmer and can reduce heating costs.

tooltips.insulationThickness: A thicker insulation layer increases the building's energy efficiency. Depending on the age of the insulation, between 4 cm and 12 cm is common.

tooltips.constructionYear: Enter the year your current heating system was installed. Older systems often work less efficiently and consume more energy.
tooltips.primaryEnergyCarrier: Select the fuel for your heating system, for example natural gas, heating oil or electricity for a heat pump.
tooltips.heatingSystemType: This refers to the device that generates the heat, e.g. a condensing boiler or a heat pump. More modern devices generally consume less energy.
tooltips.heatingSurfaceType: Radiators are the classic wall-mounted heaters. A surface heating system distributes heat through the floor, wall or ceiling and works particularly efficiently at low temperatures.

bills.consumption: What is your annual energy consumption?
bills.baseRate: What is your annual base price?

tooltips.consumption: Enter the total heating costs you incur per year. These usually include the base price and consumption costs. You can find this value on your most recent annual bill.
tooltips.unitRate: The unit rate indicates how much you pay per unit of energy consumed (e.g. €/kWh, €/L or €/kg). You can find it on your annual bill or in your energy supply contract.
tooltips.baseRate: The base price is the fixed amount you pay regardless of your actual energy consumption. You can find it on your annual bill or in your energy supply contract.

errors.baseRateExceedsTotal: The annual base price cannot be higher than your annual heating costs.
errors.unitRateMustBePositive: The unit rate must be greater than 0 when annual heating costs are provided.

electricity.title: Electricity and Renewable Energy
electricity.type: What type of electricity do you use?
electricity.consumption: What is your annual electricity consumption?
electricity.baseRate: How much is the base rate of your electricity cost?

tooltips.type: Mixed electricity contains power from various sources, including fossil fuels. Renewable electricity comes from wind, sun or water and has a significantly better CO₂ footprint.
tooltips.consumption: Enter your annual electricity consumption in kWh. You can find this value on your annual bill. An average household uses approximately 2,500–4,000 kWh per year.
tooltips.unitRate: The price you pay per kilowatt hour (kWh) of electricity. You can find this value on your electricity bill. The average price is around 30–40 cents per kWh.
tooltips.baseRate: The base rate is the fixed amount you pay regardless of your actual energy consumption. You can find it on your annual bill or in your energy supply contract.

renovation.title: Renovation Measures
renovation.subtitle: Select the measures you want to compare:

summary.title: Selected Renovation Measures
summary.hint: You can change the selection in the previous step.

tooltips.envelope_roof: Roof insulation significantly reduces heat loss through the roof and improves summer heat protection. The measure is especially effective in converted loft spaces. The calculation only applies when the loft is heated.
tooltips.envelope_topFloor: A lot of heat is often lost through the top floor ceiling. Insulating this surface is one of the simplest and most cost-effective renovation measures. The calculation only applies when the loft is unheated.
tooltips.envelope_bottomFloor: An uninsulated basement ceiling can lead to cold floors and heat loss. The insulation is comparatively inexpensive and can usually be installed with little effort.
tooltips.envelope_outerWalls: Outer walls make up a large part of the building envelope. Insulation significantly reduces heat loss and improves living comfort.
tooltips.envelope_outerWindows: Older windows often cause high heat loss and draughts. Modern energy-efficient windows with multiple glazing significantly improve energy efficiency and living comfort.
tooltips.envelope_roofWindows: Older roof windows often have high heat losses. Modern roof windows with thermal glazing reduce draughts and improve living comfort in the loft. The calculation only applies when the loft is heated.
tooltips.heat_renew: The existing heating system is replaced with a more modern and efficient system of the same type. This can reduce energy consumption and heating costs.
tooltips.heat_none_air_source_heat_pump_lt_40: An air source heat pump uses outdoor air for heating. It works especially efficiently in well-insulated buildings and reduces the need for fossil fuels.
tooltips.heat_none_ground_source_heat_pump_lt_40: A ground source heat pump uses heat from the ground. It works very efficiently but requires sufficient space and is associated with higher investment costs.
tooltips.heat_wood_pellets_standard_boiler_70_55: Wood pellets are a renewable fuel made from compressed wood waste. A pellet boiler burns them efficiently and offers a more sustainable alternative to fossil-fuel systems.
tooltips.heat_natural_gas_improved_condensing_boi: A modern condensing gas boiler recovers heat from the exhaust gas and therefore achieves significantly higher efficiency than conventional gas heating systems.
tooltips.heat_bio_gas_improved_condensing_boiler_: Biogas is produced from organic materials and is a renewable alternative to fossil natural gas. A biogas boiler significantly reduces the CO₂ footprint of your heating.
tooltips.heat_district_heating_district_heating_a: District heating supplies the building with heat energy via the existing municipal heat network. A separate heating system in the building is usually no longer required. If a connection is possible, the building can be supplied via the district heating network.
tooltips.surface_radiant_surface_heating: Instead of individual radiators, a surface heating system warms the floor, wall or ceiling in living spaces more evenly. This allows the heating to often work with lower temperatures and usually consume less energy.
tooltips.noMeasureHeating: The existing heating system remains unchanged.

export.consentDescription:
If you consent, only the data technically required for the building data donation and heat planning will be transmitted to the $t(municipality:administration.genericName). This includes, in particular, the full building address, building coordinates, building ID, and the approved input and calculation results. Because the data relates to a specific building, it is not anonymous. Registration or the provision of names and contact details is not required.

Submission is linked to downloading the PDF report and takes place when you request the report. The report also contains a randomly generated deletion link that lets you delete the submitted data after a confirmation dialog.
export.consentLabel: Yes, I would like to voluntarily provide the technically required building, input, and calculation data and contribute to climate protection in $t(municipality:name).
export.privacyNote: Data protection in accordance with GDPR Art. 6(1)(a): Your consent is voluntary and can be withdrawn at any time. The transmitted data includes the full building address and building coordinates; no name, user account, or contact details are required.

downloadItems.dataDonation: If you have shared your building data with the $t(municipality:administration.name): the dataset reduced to the submitted scope as a machine-readable file (JSON), plus your deletion link

step1.title: Get an Energy Consultation
step1.description: Use this report as the basis for a professional energy consultation. The consultation is subsidised by up to 80% of the costs (max. €1,300 for single- and two-family homes).

step2.title: Apply for Funding
step2.description: Submit funding applications before starting the measures. The energy consultant will help you select the right programmes and complete the application correctly.

step3.title: Compare Quotes
step3.description: Obtain at least three quotes from qualified specialist contractors. Pay attention to references, warranties and compliance with funding requirements.

step4.title: Carry Out Renovation
step4.description: Plan the order of measures carefully – ideally starting with the building envelope, then the technical systems. This ensures the new heating system is optimally sized.
